summary: Fares Elsabbagh, founder of Ottawa General Contractors, tells David DiNardo how a kid from subsidized housing who hated being told what to do turned a $50,000 stake and a digital marketing landing page into a design-build construction company doing $20 million a year. He walks through the near-sale at the ten-year mark, the shift from chasing sales to designing experiences for staff, subcontractors and clients, and the pivot to growth by acquisition. The back half is a practical look at Ottawa's new zoning rules and the economics of building 8 to 12-unit multiplexes, plus why both men now see AI as the same kind of opportunity digital marketing was 16 years ago.
takeaways: Sell first and build the back end after: Fares had never lifted a hammer when a construction landing page started generating leads, and the company did a million dollars in its first year by getting the sale and then figuring out delivery.

At $10 million in revenue with staff, subcontractors and homeowners all unhappy, he turned down a roughly $1 million buyout and instead rebuilt the business around delivering an experience to all three groups, which cut turnover and lifted reviews and referrals.

Growing through acquisition beat the startup route: the team wrote down the exact business profile they wanted, reached out to about 1,000 companies, took roughly 30 meetings, and used a former BDC consultant to quarterback the deal.
Under Ottawa's new zoning, almost any lot can become a multi-unit; staying at 12 units or fewer avoids site plan control, which can add $50,000 to $100,000 and an extra year or two.

A rough model for a 10-unit build on a $500,000 lot is about $2.5 million all-in, a finished value of $3 to $3.5 million, and a refinance that returns most of the investor's cash; a permit takes about six months and construction about a year.

Fares's advice to young people is to master AI now the way he mastered digital marketing in 2010: build a simple tool like an AI receptionist, give it to a business owner for free, get feedback, and grow from there.
His sticky-note rule for himself and his kids: losers look for excuses and winners look for opportunities.
